claims.text: The integrity of the native oxide film on pre-exposure Q235 steel modulates the onset of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments.
A more intact and uniform oxide film suppresses corrosion relative to a compromised oxide film.
Untreated, pre-exposure Q235 steel has a naturally formed native oxide film.
Controlled pre-exposure oxidation can alter the thickness, uniformity, and adherence of the oxide film on Q235 steel.
A high-quality, intact oxide film acts as a barrier to corrosive attack.
An intact oxide film inhibits corrosion by stabilizing the metal surface.
Compromising oxide-film integrity permits aggressive species to penetrate the surface more readily.
Greater penetration of aggressive species triggers or accelerates corrosion-related degradation.
Elevated temperature can further destabilize a weak oxide barrier.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, an improved oxide film will delay corrosion initiation.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, an improved oxide film will reduce corrosion-related degradation.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, a compromised oxide film will produce earlier corrosion onset.
Relative to untreated Q235 steel, a compromised oxide film will produce higher degradation rates.
The effect of oxide-film integrity on degradation will be more pronounced at 60–80°C than at approximately 25°C because of enhanced chemical kinetics.
